name: Depilatory cream

lead: A depilatory cream is a topical product, typically containing thioglycolate salts, that dissolves hair at the skin surface so it can be wiped away. It is used on legs, chest and other areas without needing a blade.
It is painless, and results last a few days, similar to shaving. Patch testing is advised because the chemicals are irritating.

paras: Alkaline thioglycolate breaks the disulfide bonds of keratin, weakening the hair shaft so it can be scraped off with the cream.

Irritant contact dermatitis and chemical burns are the main risks, especially when left longer than directed or applied on broken or recently waxed skin. A pediatric case report documents severe irritant reaction after waxing and depilatory use. Evidence is limited to case reports and reviews.

lead: A depilatory cream is a topical product that removes hair chemically. Most contain thioglycolate salts, which are commonly described as weakening the keratin of the hair shaft so that the hair can be wiped or scraped from the skin surface [1]. It is sold for the legs, underarms, bikini area, face and torso, including men's formulations for the chest and other body hair.

Hair removal reviews classify chemical depilatories, along with shaving, as depilation: removal of the hair shaft only, without removing the follicle [2][3]. All methods other than electrolysis are described as temporary [3]. Hair removed at the surface typically regrows within days.

The most extensive clinical research on depilatory creams is not cosmetic: a series of randomized and controlled trials compared cream depilation with shaving for preparing the skin before surgery, and Cochrane reviews have assessed these trials [4][5][6][7][8][9][10]. For cosmetic use, the literature consists mostly of case reports, laboratory studies of skin effects and general reviews.

paras: Depilatory creams are alkaline emulsions. The usual active ingredients are thioglycolate salts, such as calcium or potassium thioglycolate, which are commonly described as breaking the disulfide bonds that give keratin its strength, so that the softened hair can be wiped or scraped away. A 2008 laboratory study describes thioglycolate as the active ingredient of depilatory creams [1]. A French formulation paper described optimising a cold-process emulsion of calcium thioglycolate [11].

Because the chemistry acts on hair keratin and also affects skin keratin, the product is left on for a limited time specified by the manufacturer. A 2008 laboratory study applied a depilatory cream to fresh human skin for ten minutes and examined the changes in the stratum corneum; it characterised thioglycolate as a penetration enhancer and raised the possibility that it could increase permeation of other substances across skin [1]. A 2019 in vitro study similarly examined how physical and chemical hair removal methods affect skin barrier function [12].

Hair removal reviews place depilatory creams in the same temporary category as shaving, with each method having advantages and disadvantages in efficacy and adverse events [3]. In the clinical trials of preoperative skin preparation, creams were studied as an alternative to shaving. A 1976 British Medical Journal trial of cream depilation versus routine shaving reported a similar wound infection rate in both groups, and found cream depilation effective, atraumatic and able to be self-administered, with a reduction in skin-surface bacteria and lower cost than shaving [13]. A randomized trial comparing razor shaving with a depilatory cream for preoperative preparation has also been published from Nigeria [8].
These trials measure infection outcomes in surgical patients, not the cosmetic quality or duration of hair removal.

Irritant contact dermatitis is the main reported harm in the sources reviewed, and chemical burns are described in consumer and clinical guidance, particularly with application longer than directed or on broken or recently treated skin. A 2019 Pediatric Dermatology case report described severe irritant contact dermatitis after sequential waxing and depilatory cream use [14].

Laboratory work published in 2022 in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology examined the role of epidermal fatty acid-binding protein in acute skin inflammation induced by depilatories [15]. Product labels commonly advise a patch test before first use and avoidance of broken or irritated skin; these are label-based safety instructions rather than findings of the cited studies.

Cochrane reviews of preoperative hair removal (first published 2006, updated in 2011 and 2021) examined whether removing hair before surgery affects surgical site infection and whether the method matters [4][5][6][7]. Primary trials of depilatory creams date from 1966 onward [16][13][17][18][8], and a 2017 meta-analysis in the Journal of Clinical Nursing compared preoperative hair removal methods for surgical site infection [19]. Conclusions on cream versus other methods are given in the full reviews; the abstract available for the 2021 update describes its aim of assessing hair removal versus no removal, and the method, timing and setting of removal [4].

Depilatory creams are discussed in grooming circles as a painless, blade-free way to remove body hair from the chest, legs and other areas, often by people whose skin reacts to razors. The site's own rating notes that results last a few days, similar to shaving, and that patch testing is commonly advised given the irritation potential.

Human trials of depilatory cream have mostly been done in surgical preparation. A 1966 Medical Journal of Australia trial, a 1976 British Medical Journal controlled trial, a 1983 American Journal of Surgery randomized trial comparing shaving with depilatory cream, a 2011 randomized trial in the Journal of Infection in Developing Countries and a 2020 randomized trial in the Nigerian Journal of Clinical Practice all examined cream depilation in patients [13][16][17][18][8]. Several Cochrane reviews pooled the evidence on preoperative hair removal [4][5][6][7]. For purely cosmetic use, a 2019 case report and laboratory skin-barrier studies are the available human-relevant literature [14][1][12].
